Andrey Zvyagintsev on Marriage, Mythology, and the Violence of Family Life

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the emotional punch in the gut of Andrey Zvyagintsev’s debut feature, The Return (2003), about an estranged father who takes his two teenage sons on a camping trip, has remained with me, even though I first saw it more than twenty years ago at the Toronto Film Festival.
  • Industry observers note that based on Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969), Minotaur, for the most part, is an intimate family drama.
  • The story unfolds methodically and slowly in the family’s gorgeous home surrounded by trees, on quiet city streets, and in Galina’s lover’s apartment—until it erupts into violence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the emotional punch in the gut of Andrey Zvyagintsev’s debut feature, The Return (2003), about an estranged father who takes his two teenage sons on a camping trip, has remained with me, even though I first saw it more than twenty years ago at the Toronto Film Festival. Since then, Zvyagintsev has directed five more films, two of which—Leviathan (2014) and Loveless (2017)—were nominated for Best Foreign Language Film at the Academy Awards. His most recent feature, Minotaur (2026), which is set against the backdrop of mobilization for the war in Ukraine, won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival.

Industry observers note that based on Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969), Minotaur, for the most part, is an intimate family drama. Successful businessman Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) suspects his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) of having an affair. Their son, Seryozha, is being bullied at school, and the mayor of the fictional Russian city where the film is set, demands that business owners provide him with a list of employees to be conscripted as soldiers—essentially, cannon fodder.

The story unfolds methodically and slowly in the family’s gorgeous home surrounded by trees, on quiet city streets, and in Galina’s lover’s apartment—until it erupts into violence.

Zvyagintsev lives in France and is at the moment at work on a new film (that I thought was called Jupiter—more details below) about a Russian oligarch. We spoke on Zoom via a translator. The interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

A heads up: possible spoilers in the discussion.

Radha Vatsal: I want to start with some general observations: that fathers, wealth or power, and violence, often in the form of unexpected deaths, seem to be a theme that crop up frequently in your films. But there’s also a mythical dimension that we’ve seen in some of the titles like Minotaur and Leviathan, and I’m curious what draws you to this mythical element.

Recent findings suggest that andrey Zvyagintsev: Only two out of six films have a mythological reference—Leviathan and Minotaur. Only two.

AZ: Jupiter, no, it’s a working title.

RV: Okay. All right, so then maybe–.

Industry observers note that AZ: Jupiter is a name we no longer aim to use because in the Venice Film Festival this year, there was a film named Jupiter. So we could no longer use that name. They did it faster than we could.

[But to answer your question,] Minotaur, the film, has two sides to it. One is a personal family story, and the other is a story about society. So we could say that there are two films inside Minotaur, and they both have a very strong connection to each other. And they are represented in the title “Minotaur.”.

Well, the first one, as you know from Greek mythology, is the mythological monster that lives in the labyrinth and demands human sacrifices. And then the other part, the more intimate family side—Balzac has a work called “The Physiology of Marriage” [1829] and the subtitle is “Meditations.” The interesting thing is that Balzac was twenty-five when he wrote that work. He was a very, very young man, and it’s really astonishing that someone so young has such an insight into family and married life.

There is a part where Balzac writes that marital life is like a labyrinth, where the husband wanders in anxiety and watches over his wife. And the husband experiences anxiety when he sees ambiguity, secrets, something unknown in the wife, and he waits anxiously in case there might be a lover around the corner of the labyrinth.

Industry observers note that and there is a phrase that Balzac writes, and I’m going to try to quote it to you: That while the husband is wandering around the labyrinth, he’s waiting for the lover to jump out from around the corner; and the lover “minotaurizes”—so making minotaur into a verb—the husband. “Minotaurizes”—that’s the word Balzac uses.

The metaphor is quite simple because for Balzac to give the husband horns, as the minotaur has horns, means to cheat on the husband. But I think it’s also interesting that we do not know what this encounter will entail, and the lover may very well be also the victim of the situation.

So to go back to your question, the title works in two respects and has two sides and explanations to it.

Industry observers note that RV: I wanted to discuss the use of interior space in Minotaur. I was very struck by the house. Like the apartment in Elena [Zyvagintsev’s domestic/crime drama from 2011], Gleb and Galina’s home feels like its own character in the film. And there’s a lot of glass and expensive surfaces. It’s also very restrained and tasteful, and it doesn’t match up to the idea we have in the west of fresh money in Russia being very flashy and in your face.

So I was wondering if you could talk about how you center their home, and also your choice of the décor in their home and the restraint.

AZ: I can tell you that new money—especially the Russians, you can obviously find some crazy mansions and different manifestations of wealth. Much more ostentatious. This house is probably worth $2 to $3 million, which is not a lot of money for a really wealthy Russian businessman.

It was incredibly lucky to encounter a house like this in Riga, in Latvia, where we were shooting, because most houses there have this very European kind of look to them, which is not the style of houses you can find in Russia. And so this house was definitely an exception, and we were lucky to find it.

In a recent development, and in the case of Elena, both Elena’s apartment with Vladimir, her husband, and the apartment where her son Seryozha lives with his family—it was all built for the film. In the case of the house you see in Minotaur, this is a house that belongs to the architect who built it, and he actually lives in it. And the only set that was built for Minotaur is the apartment of Anton, the lover. That’s a studio apartment that was built specifically for the film.

Industry observers note that RV: The extended sequence of violence that takes place halfway through the film, without any dialogue, is so engrossing. And I was wondering whether that whole sequence was planned or was some of it improvised? It feels like it takes place in real time.

It has been revealed that AZ: It was not improvised at all. It was fully planned beat by beat because every scene that involves blood is automatically very hard to do because you have to wash the blood away after every take and then re-spill it. So it takes a lot of time and effort to do that.

According to recent reports, so, as I said, we planned everything well in advance and in a very detailed manner. And we spent five days shooting at the apartment. So day one was love scenes between Galina and her lover. The second day was the encounter between the lover and the husband; and then days three, four, five were all dedicated to the murder scene and the aftermath. So we gave our guy one day to enjoy love, and then the other days, he was getting murdered.

Sources indicate that RV: Gleb’s advice to Seryozha when Seryozha tells him that he’s being bullied at school. I expected Glib to be more brutal, and I was surprised that he gave him quite mild advice of how to deal with the bullies.

AZ: You seem to be the only person to think it was mild advice. Where are you from?

RV: India, but I live in Fresh York.

AZ:  Russia is a very patriarchal country, and this is how it happens there. The man is the head of the family. And some 100 years ago, children were not even allowed to start eating before the father starts. And if they did, they could be struck with a wooden spoon on their forehead. So this is regarded by many as a normal form of communication between father and children in Russia.

And, this is an important detail: Gleb starts with saying you have to grab [the bully] by the collar, but then he indicates, do not touch him, but just say with the same expression, tell him very deliberately, if you do something like this one more time… So the advice has two parts to it.

I’m not entirely sure what the tool is against bullying at school and the way children sometimes relate to each other in an angry or violent manner. It’s a difficult conversation. So, it’s hard to tell what the right reaction would be.

According to recent reports, this situation is very strange for me. If you have better advice on what to do if a child is getting bullied at school, I would love to hear it because I have a teenage son who is at school in France, in a boarding school, and he also had a problem with bullying, and I also had to give him some advice. My advice was more delicate, but I did explain to him that you have to face the person who tries to bully you and, you know, at least have a conversation.

And going back to your first question about my titles having a mythological connotation, I made a joke earlier about Venice, you know, having a film in competition that was named Jupiter.

Sources indicate that but the truth is, I thought to myself that I probably have a few too many mythological titles. So my fresh film will be called something else, which I cannot tell you right now, but it will be something much better and much more interesting.

RV: Thank you very much. I look forward to seeing it.

Radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The Upcoming York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

Tech Report: Beyond Lupin: The Brazen Gentlemen Thieves of Fiction

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums.
  • Industry observers note that he models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc.
  • Diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums. His meticulously planned heists are executed with a showman’s flair. The anti-hero of the hit Netflix series Lupin, portrayed to perfection by actor Omar Sy, Diop dons elaborate disguises, slips into fake identities, and turns on the charm as he swipes priceless gems and outwits the police.

Industry observers note that he models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc. Lupin made his debut in 1905, at the height of the glamorous Belle Époque, and was featured in two dozen novels and short story collections. A skilled burglar and a master of disguise, this impish shapeshifter relishes the challenge of stealing the un-stealable and often returns the treasures he pilfers. He’s more interested in righting wrongs than living off ill-gotten gains. So is Diop – he’s determined to exonerate his father, who was wrongly accused of stealing a priceless necklace from the powerful and corrupt businessman Hubert Pellegrini.

Diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023. As Lupin returns for a long-anticipated fourth season, here’s a lineup of five of the slickest gentlemen thieves of fiction:.

A.J. Raffles: Lupin was France’s answer to a wildly popular English thief of fiction. In 1898, E. W. Hornung (the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle) published the first of twenty-six stories on the adventures of Arthur Raffles, a London man-about-town and star cricket player who steals to support his expensive lifestyle and keep up appearances. His speciality is cracking safes and he enlists a sidekick from his school days, Bunny Manders, as a partner-in-crime.

It has been revealed that despite his crooked side-gig, Raffles adheres to a gentlemanly moral code. He shudders at the thought of preying on a host or a friend, and rarely packs a gun when he sets out to steal. “It would be very awkward if anything went wrong,” he tells Manders. “One might use it, and that’s not the game at all.” He stalks the corrupt and the obscenely wealthy, reasoning that “the immorally rich” are the logical targets for a “richly immoral” thief like himself.

Sources indicate that hercule Flambeau: His name may sound like that of a certain Belgian detective, but Flambeau’s obsession is stealing jewels, not solving crimes. That changes after a run-in with a priest and part-time detective dreamed up by writer G.K. Chesterton. In the first Father Brown short story, “The Blue Cross,” published in 1910, the clergyman with a kindly demeanor and a keen sense of human nature foils Flambeau’s attempt to steal a religious relic.

Sources indicate that like Lupin, Flambeau is one of France’s most-wanted criminals – Chesterton described him as a “colossus of crime” with a long record of “ingenious and wholesale robbery.” And like Lupin, he can disguise himself and hide in plain sight, despite being over six feet tall. He is also “a startling acrobat,” wrote his creator, who “could leap like a grasshopper and melt into the tree-tops like a monkey.” Flambeau became a recurring character, appearing in more than a dozen of the fifty-three Father Brown stories, and not only reforms but eventually helps the clergyman to crack cases.

Industry observers note that john Robie: It’s the early 1950s on the French Riviera and Robie, a wily burglar whose agility earned him the nickname “Le Chat” before he was caught and imprisoned, is forced out of retirement when a copycat makes him a suspect in upcoming crimes. The protagonist in American travel writer David Dodge’s 1952 novel To Catch a Thief sets out to trap his doppelgänger.

Robie is the consummate gentleman thief – dashing, clever, a master of his calling. Who better to portray him when Alfred Hitchcock brought the story to the substantial screen in 1955 than the king of suave, Cary Grant. “For what it’s worth,” Grant-as-Robie points out in a line added for the movie, “I never stole from anybody who would go hungry.”.

Sir Charles Lytton: Peter Sellers’s hilariously inept Inspector Jacques Clouseau debuted in the 1963 movie The Pink Panther, but the real star of the blockbuster franchise’s first instalment was David Niven. He was cast as the debonaire playboy Sir Charles Lytton, who leads a double life as an elusive jewel thief known as “The Phantom.” Niven was an inspired choice – he played Raffles on screen in 1939, in one of many films to feature Hornung’s character.

It has been revealed that the Pink Panther is reputed to be the world’s largest diamond and Lytton has come to a ski resort in the Italian Alps to steal it. The bumbling Clouseau is there to try to stop him. Niven may have enjoyed top billing as a classy crook but Sellers’s over-the-top performance stole the show and hijacked the franchise.

In a recent development, danny Ocean: Frank Sinatra was the first to tackle the role of the ringleader of a gang of thieves who rob five Las Vegas casinos on Fresh Year’s Eve in the 1960 movie Ocean’s 11. George Clooney revived the character four decades later in 2001’s Ocean’s Eleven, with Danny assembling a team of skilled crooks (an all-star cast that includes Brad Pitt and Matt Damon) to loot a supposedly impregnable Vegas vault.

The movie inspired two sequels, with the gang reuniting to steal a Fabergé egg in Ocean’s Twelve and a casino’s cash and a trove of diamonds in Ocean’s Thirteen. In each movie the targets are fellow thieves or ruthless, unscrupulous moguls. The heists are filled with Lupin-worthy disguises and deceptions and Clooney is a natural for the modern iteration of the cool, classy crook.

Industry observers note that it’s little wonder the gentleman thief is a staple of fiction. His victims are fellow travellers who deserve to be cut down to size, or have insurance policies or pockets deep enough to absorb their losses. Admiring their audacity and cheering them on is a guilty pleasure we can all enjoy.

Dean Jobb’s latest true crime book, A Gentleman and a Thief: The Daring Jewel Heists of a Jazz Age Rogue (Algonquin Books and HarperCollins Canada), is a Newly introduced York Times Editors’ Choice and a national bestseller in Canada. It’s the story of Arthur Barry, who charmed the elite of 1920s New York City while planning and executing some of the most brazen jewel thefts in history. Find him at deanjobb.com.

    Major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a new market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses.

    Cravath, Swaine & Moore’s associate salary scale was increased Tuesday, and it rivals the raises declared in June at Milbank, according to coverage by Reuters.

    According to recent reports, milbank increased the associate salary range from $235,000 to $455,000. In July, it offered special bonuses between $6,000 and $25,000 for associates. Reuters is also reporting pay increases at Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton.

    Cravath’s special bonuses—$11,000 to $40,000—based on class year, exceeded Milbank’s scale. Its year-end bonus scale starts at $15,000 and extends to $115,000, which is a continuation of what the firm and others offered in past years.

    No comments were given by Cravath.

    • It has been revealed that today the Department of Justice unveiled coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • In a recent development, “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • According to recent reports, “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that today the Department of Justice unveiled coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    In a recent development, “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement reveals that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    According to recent reports, “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    It has been revealed that “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” mentioned First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure indicates that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” noted U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    Industry observers note that “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” remarked FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    Sources indicate that “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California revealed the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    Sources indicate that the North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    It has been revealed that efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, as Tubi looks to bring more creators to its shores, it is helping them solve a prevalent problem by providing easier access to capital. That’s the gist of the $250,000 Tubi x Kickstarter Fandom Fund, which unites a Fox-owned streaming service and a 17-year-old crowdfunding platform.

    According to recent reports, the Fandom Fund follows up last year’s FilmStream Collective, a partnership between Tubi and Kickstarter that delivered support to more than 20 independent films. The upcoming collab between the companies will function similarly; Tubi will throw its weight behind active Kickstarter campaigns, which it will distribute exclusively.

    Sources indicate that tubi won’t just pick any Kickstarter project; instead, as it has done with its other incubator programs, it will hone in on the genres that have the widest appeal among its 110 million monthly active users. The categories fitting that description include horror, YA, Black entertainment, true crime, LGBTQ+, comedy, and reality.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    It has been revealed that per Business Insider, $150,000 of the fund will be split between eight to 15 Kickstarter campaigns. The remaining $100,000 will go in one lump sum to a larger project.

    For Kickstarter, the Fandom Fund represents an increasing commitment to the creator economy. It is part of the three-month-old Culture Fund, which builds on Kickstarter’s enduring status as a key tool for indie artists. In 2024 alone, the platform generated over $700 million of fundraising across more than 35,000 projects.

    Indie creators don’t always get distribution deals with brand-name platforms, but Tubi is eager to support the next generation of storytellers — whom it believes are just as capable as traditional TV voices. To that end, Tubi has premiered a handful of indicates and movies led by social media standouts. One of the projects in the Fandom Fund will get a similar treatment by receiving additional backing, allowing it to be developed into a full-length series or feature film.

    Sources indicate that “We believe great talent can come from anywhere,” said Tubi GM of Creator Programs and EVP of Business Development Rich Bloom in a statement. “The Fandom Fund gives emerging storytellers the resources to bring those ambitious ideas to life on a bigger canvas while preserving the creative voice, vision and ownership that made their work resonate.”.

    According to recent reports, kickstarter will provide updates about the Fandom Fund through its film-focused newsletter. Participation in the fund requires an active campaign, so if you want Tubi’s backing, get your crowdfunding game on.

    According to recent reports, kirkland & Ellis has provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies, according to U.S. congressional Democrats in a statement released Thursday. (Image from Shutterstock).

    Kirkland & Ellis has provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies, according to U.S. congressional Democrats in a statement released Thursday.

    In a recent development, democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate are increasing their scrutiny of nine major law firms’ agreements with the Trump administration last year to provide nearly $1 billion in free legal services. The agreements allowed the firms to avoid executive orders targeting their legal work, political affiliations and diversity policies.

    Kirkland & Ellis performed about $4 million in pro ​bono work for the Commerce Department, as well as $2.2 million for the Defense Department, according to a statement by several Democrats in the Senate and House of Representatives.

    The firm also provided free legal services to the Postal Service and the ​International Development Finance Corporation, according to a story by Reuters.

    According to recent reports, kirkland & Ellis turned down requests to work on specific projects for the Trump administration, including the renaming of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and challenges to the Postal Service’s handling of mail ballots, according to a story by CBS News.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that pirated content has been an issue for Meta for so long that it was still known as Facebook when creators first fought back against so-called “freebooters.” To combat unauthorized reuploads, Meta brought a “content protection” tool to Facebook last year. Now, Instagram creators are getting access to that resource as well.

    “Eligible creators” on Instagram can now enroll for access to the management system that was previously limited to Facebook. Like Facebook’s video rights manager, which was itself adapted from previous services like YouTube’s Content ID, the content protection tool uses fingerprinting technology to scan for uploads that are identical to an enrolled creator’s video.

    Recent findings suggest that once a match is detected, Instagrammers can respond in one of four different ways: They can track the reupload (that’s the default option), request for it to be hidden, require the reuploader to add a credit link, or release their claim on the infringing video. Notably, creators cannot receive monetization through the reposts, as is possible through services like Content ID.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Sources indicate that meta has positioned itself as a champion of original, non-repetitive content. It updated Instagram’s algorithm, providing more visibility for creators who share their own work. Financial penalties for serial reuploaders came to Facebook in 2025, and further penalties arrived on Instagram this year.

    In a recent development, other platforms have followed Meta’s lead. YouTube cracked down on “mass-produced or repetitive” content in 2025. Earlier this year, Google’s video hub clarified that creators aren’t able to monetize “generic” uploads. Anything “unsatisfying or off-putting” — i.e. the sort of slop you’d expected a generative AI model to spit out — faced similar repercussions.

    Industry observers note that the link between unoriginal reuploads and AI slop is undeniable. Traditional studios have urged platforms to crack down on channels that use AI to steal from artists rather than executing original concepts. Those demands have led to new rules across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram.

    Recent findings suggest that by bringing content protection to Instagram, Meta is setting itself up to take further action against AI slop in the future. An introductory post explains that “we’re also exploring different ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly,” so stay tuned for that if you’re sick of low-effort AI posts.

    #21175. The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1742 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.
    • This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known.
    • The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

    This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

    First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

    This process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal matter in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

    Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

    Industry observers note that as noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

    Industry observers note that nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an notable issue of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

    This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an matter that has been turned down one or more times.

    Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

    The answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

    But much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 states the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an important issue of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

    Just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

    Recent findings suggest that the cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

    Sources indicate that and the justices rarely discuss it. In his new book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

    Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

    Industry observers note that many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

    It has been revealed that the clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

    It has been revealed that caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

    It has been revealed that question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

    According to recent reports, the number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

    Oddly, no one seems to know why.

    There are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

    These interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

    Different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer new laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

    It has been revealed that it is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a company based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the matter (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

    According to recent reports, question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal issues, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

    A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

    Industry observers note that the process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

    Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.

    Recommended Citation: Stephen Wermiel, The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 12, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-sometimes-straightforward-sometimes-befuddling-certiorari-process/.

    #21174. Tech Report: What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2417 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • Industry observers note that on Oct.
    • Sources indicate that in all of these cases, including this one, the policies at issue are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    Industry observers note that on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case is one of several in recent years dealing with magnet school admissions policies. While prior cases addressed the constitutional permissibility of changes to selection criteria at some of the nation’s most sought after public high schools like the Thomas Jefferson High School in northern Virginia and Stuyvesant High School and Bronx High School of Science in New York City, this case addresses whether changes to selection criteria for middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County, Maryland violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment.

    Sources indicate that in all of these cases, including this one, the policies at issue are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process. As a result, the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard is not directly relevant. In that case, the court held that using race as an explicit factor in the admissions process was unconstitutional.

    At problem in this case is a change from one facially neutral admissions policy to another. During the pandemic, the school adopted the so-called “Pandemic Strategy.” Under the Pandemic Plan, all students are considered for admission to magnet schools if they meet minimum grade requirements and if their locally compared state assessment scores exceed a cut-off. Admission is then determined by a lottery from among those students who meet these requirements. Because schools in the region differ in their racial composition, basing admissions decisions on how well students score relative to other students in their same school ultimately affects the demographic composition of admitted students. AFEF claims that the Pandemic Plan violates equal protection because Montgomery County adopted it in order to change the racial demographics of the magnet schools and the plan had the effect of decreasing the share of Asian-American and white students.

    Sources indicate that according to the approach used by all of the courts evaluating magnet school admission practices, these facially neutral policies only violate equal protection if they are adopted for an impermissible reason (the intent element) and produce a discriminatory effect (the effect element). In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the district court found that the plaintiff had not alleged facts sufficient to satisfy either prong and so the school board’s motion to dismiss was granted. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit affirmed on the grounds that the district court properly evaluated whether there was a discriminatory effect.

    Industry observers note that when and why facially neutral policies violate equal protection is a hotly contested matter. Consider first the intent element. While all agree that the intention to exclude members of a particular racial group is invidious, there is disagreement about whether the intent to increase racial diversity is also impermissible. The Supreme Court has not yet directly ruled on this crucial issue and will not do so in this case. The cert grant in AFEF v. Montgomery County focuses only on the second element: the discriminatory effect. In particular, the Supreme Court limited its grant of AFEF’s petition to the following question: “Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.”.

    This framing of the question roughly tracks the debate in the circuits between two different ways of showing discriminatory effect. In order to illustrate, let’s set aside the intent prong and assume it has been satisfied, either because the policy was actually adopted in order to reduce the percentage of Asian or white students in the magnet schools (though this fact is in dispute) or because the intention to increase the racial diversity of the schools is an impermissible intention (though this legal claim is contested). According to the 4th Circuit in Coalition for TJ v. Fairfax County and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit in Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence Corp. v. School Committee for the City of Boston, the effect element would be satisfied if a lower percentage of Asian or white students are admitted than applied. For example, if Asian students represent 30% of the applicant pool but only 20% of the admitted class, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. However, if 40% of the admitted class are Asian, then no discriminatory effect would be found because Asian students would in this case constitute a higher percentage of the admitted class than their 30% share in the applicant pool. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, both the district court and the 4th Circuit followed this approach.

    By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit in Sargent v. School District of Philadelphia, the dissenting judge in Coalition for TJ, and Justice Samuel Alito in his dissent from the denial of cert. in that case, assess discriminatory effect differently. Rather than compare the percentage of admitted students of the race alleged to be intentionally excluded to their percentage in the wider applicant pool, these jurists look to see if there has been a decrease in the percentage of admitted students of this race under the new policy as compared to the prior policy. When a meaningful decrease is present, this constitutes a discriminatory effect. For example, if 50% of the admitted class were Asian under the prior policy and 40% are Asian under the new policy, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. And this would be so even if Asian students are still “overrepresented” in the sense that the percentage admitted is higher than their percentage of the applicant pool (30% in this example). In an article evaluating each of these approaches, we call this second approach the “Before-After Comparison” or “BAC,” and we call the first approach the “Population Comparison” or “PC.”.

    Yet both the PC and the BAC, as means of assessing discriminatory effect, have significant flaws. Let’s begin with the PC – the test used by the 4th and 1st Circuits. Recall that because the doctrine requires both impermissible intent and a discriminatory effect, it requires something more than just the fact that a policy is chosen for an invidious reason. The PC would effectively allow deliberate attempts to exclude Asians so long as they do well enough overall and do not fall below their share of the applicant pool. That seems problematic.

    Next consider the BAC, the test adopted by the 3rd Circuit, on which the discriminatory effect prong is satisfied only if the percentage of Asian students declines under the fresh policy. This test puts a strong thumb on the scale in favor of existing policies, whatever their merits, since sticking with the same policy is unlikely to result in major changes in the demographics of who is admitted. Thus a decision to keep things the same will evade scrutiny. And this is so even when maintaining a policy is done for uncontroversially bad reasons (say, because the existing policy is known to admit fewer Asian students, for example). In addition, the test is oversensitive to any changes in policy, since such changes are likely to lead to demographic shifts among the admitted students and thereby trigger a decrease for some group. While it is true that there will only be an equal protection violation if the school board at problem intended this decrease, it remains the case that any change at all is risky because the effect element will likely always be satisfied for some group. For both these reasons, the BAC privileges the status quo and makes change difficult by making the status quo policy the normative baseline.

    The use of the term “aggregate” in the question on which certiorari was granted suggests that the court might think that the PC approach is flawed because it looks at how groups are treated rather than at how individuals are treated. And indeed it does. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the discriminatory effect element would be satisfied (using the PC) if the percentage of Asian and white students admitted was lower than the percentage of these groups among the fifth-grade students in the county. But the BAC is no different in this respect. It too looks at how a racial group fares under the Pandemic Proposal. The BAC would find discriminatory effect if the percentage of Asian students admitted under the Pandemic Plan is less than the percentage admitted under the approach that preceded it. In other words, both tests for discriminatory effect focus on how the racial groups who are alleged to be the target of the invidious intentions fare as groups.

    Sources indicate that can either of these tests be reframed in ways that focus on how an individual is treated, rather than how members of her racial group are treated? After all, equal protection doctrine has long emphasized that the clause protects individuals rather than groups. Unfortunately, this is not easy to do. If a school uses race to decide which students to admit, it makes sense to say that a student’s race played a role in how she was treated. Facially neutral policies are different, however. Consider a simple and familiar facially neutral policy. Suppose a school board decides to admit the top 2% of each middle school to its coveted magnet high school. Suppose also that it does so, at least in part, to increase the racial diversity of the magnet school. Because there are more black and Latino students in some middle schools and more Asian and white students in others, this policy then produces a magnet school class that has a significant number of students of all races, let us suppose. Now consider an Asian student who is denied admissions because she is not in the top 2% of her middle school class. Has she been denied admission “because of her race?”.

    Industry observers note that one answer to this question could be simply “no.” Any student rejected by the admissions policy suffers a harm. It is this harm that gives the student standing to sue. But this rejection is not based on the student’s race when the school’s admissions policy is facially neutral. If this is correct (and if aggregate tests are out), then the court’s only option is to jettison the effect prong of the claim altogether. Were the court to take this route, facially neutral laws or policies would violate equal protection solely on the grounds that they were adopted with invidious intent.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 2nd Circuit attempts a different approach. It uses the BAC to explain how individual students have suffered a discriminatory effect under a facially neutral policy. In Chinese American Citizens Alliance of Greater Fresh York v. Adams, the percentage of Asian students admitted under the challenged admissions policy remained higher than their percentage in the applicant pool (thus failing to satisfy the PC in its aggregate form) and also did not decrease as compared to the prior admissions policy (thus failing to satisfy the BAC in its aggregate form). Yet the 2nd Circuit held that the effect element “can be satisfied by proof of an adverse harm to one or more individuals based on their race that has resulted from that discriminatory law or policy” (emphasis added). But the crucial question remains: in what way were the rejected Asian students rejected “because of their race” when race did not affect these decisions since the policy is facially neutral? The 2nd Circuit answers that question by referring to the fact that these students were “qualified for admission on an individual basis under the previous criteria" (emphasis added). In other words, in the view of the 2nd Circuit, if a new policy is adopted to exclude Asian students, then those Asian students who would have been admitted under the previous policy are denied admission because of their race.

    According to recent reports, this approach can be understood as an attempt to make the BAC individualized: the court here is determining whether a student’s rejection constitutes a distinctively discriminatory harm by drawing a comparison with how she would have fared under the previous policy. If this approach works (which we are agnostic about) for the BAC, a similar approach can be tailored for the PC as well. Here is how that would go. If a facially neutral policy was adopted in order to exclude Asian students and that policy is one under which Asian students are admitted at lower rates than students of other races, then each Asian student subject to that policy is subject to a policy that makes it harder for them to be admitted than it is for students of other races. On this view, each Asian student denied admission using this policy is then denied admission based on their race.

    Thus, both tests can be articulated such that they capture a way that individual students are rejected based on their race. For this reason, the court should not choose one approach over the other on the grounds that one frames the injury in individual terms and the other looks at how groups are treated.

    Recent findings suggest that this leaves the court with two options. First, as mentioned earlier, it could jettison the effect prong of the claim entirely and conclude that bad intentions alone render a facially neutral admissions policy impermissible. Doing so would put more pressure on the importance of answering the question of what intentions are invidious and, in particular, whether the intent to increase racial diversity is itself unconstitutional. Alternatively, the court must confront the question of discriminatory harm head-on and assess whether the BAC or PC provides the better account of it.

    Deborah Hellman is the Robert E. Scott Distinguished Professor of Law and the Honorable Albert V. Bryan Jr. ’50 Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, as well as Director of their Center for Law & Philosophy.

    Lily Hu is an Assistant Professor of Philosophy at Yale University and also a contributing editor at Boston Review.

    Recommended Citation: Deborah Hellman & Lily Hu , What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 12, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/what-is-a-discriminatory-effect-the-montgomery-county-case-and-unpacking-when-schools-may-try-fo/.

    As Netflix and Disney sniff around, YouTube hypes its creators’ “world-class, studio-quality” programming at L.A. Premieres event

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tonight, YouTube brought back its film-festival-style event, Creator Premieres, to showcase a fresh batch of “world-class, studio-quality creator programming” coming exclusively to its platform.
    • According to recent reports, last year’s Creator Premieres–the first YouTube held–took place at New York City’s historic screening space Metrograph and demonstrated off projects from creators like Ms.
    • This year’s edition was hosted by House Guest‘s Scott Evans at The Hollywood Roosevelt in L.A., and highlighted upcoming projects from YouTube OGs and greats like Emma Chamberlain, Nick DiGiovanni, Lilly Singh, Wesley Wang, Grace Reiter, and more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tonight, YouTube brought back its film-festival-style event, Creator Premieres, to showcase a fresh batch of “world-class, studio-quality creator programming” coming exclusively to its platform.

    According to recent reports, last year’s Creator Premieres–the first YouTube held–took place at New York City’s historic screening space Metrograph and demonstrated off projects from creators like Ms. Rachel, Brave Wilderness, Dhar Mann, Deestroying, and Cleo Abram.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    This year’s edition was hosted by House Guest‘s Scott Evans at The Hollywood Roosevelt in L.A., and highlighted upcoming projects from YouTube OGs and greats like Emma Chamberlain, Nick DiGiovanni, Lilly Singh, Wesley Wang, Grace Reiter, and more.

    Google President Sean Downey took the stage to highlight YouTube’s continued dominance on TV screens, and gave a nod to participating creators for fueling the UGC machine that keeps viewers coming back to YouTube–on TVs and across other devices.

    Of course, he also appealed to advertisers in the same breath, reminding them that this “world-class” content is what they could be marketing alongside, if they cough up the cash to Google.

    “YouTube creators are not just shaping modern culture, they are redefining the entire entertainment landscape. This slate of reveals demonstrates how creators are commanding primetime attention on the massive screen and building unmatched fan loyalty,” Downey said. “For brands, this isn’t about buying thirty seconds of ad space; it’s about moving past standard commercial breaks and partnering directly with the storytellers who are defining modern culture.”.

    YouTube has spent years at the top of TV watch time charts–a fact that really gets under the skin of competitor Netflix. Up till recently, though, Netflix’s main response to this irritant was talking a lot of sh*t about YouTube and occasionally signing back catalog deals with view-drivers like Ms. Rachel and CoComelon.

    Industry observers note that but in the last 12 months, something’s shifted. Netflix has begun tapping creators like Salish Matter, Alan Chikin Chow, and the Stokes Twins not for back catalog agreements, but for development deals–deals which result in exclusive original programming that won’t appear on YouTube.

    And YouTube’s not happy about it. The platform has been offering creators money, including production financing and sweet ad deals, in exchange for turning down offers from Netflix. Conversely, creators who decide to sign with Netflix are put on YouTube’s naughty list, and denied perks like revenue shares from primo ad deals.

    (That being stated, Netflix-friendly creators aren’t entirely blacklisted. DiGiovanni signed a catalog crossposting deal with Netflix in July, and was still one of the headline creators at tonight’s showcase.).

    The point we’re making here is this: With Netflix–and Disney–sniffing around, YouTube has more incentive than ever to hype up its creators and their projects on a significant stage.

    So that’s exactly what it’s doing.

    Nick DiGiovanni | Chef | New series live now on a dedicated YouTube channel.

    Chef Nick DiGiovanni, the creator behind the world’s largest food YouTube channel, launches Chef (@Chef) – a new series from his production firm, Knife Drop Studios. After reaching billions of viewers through his global culinary adventures (@NickDiGiovanni) and step-by-step recipes (@NicksKitchen), DiGiovanni is now turning the camera solely toward fellow professional chefs, offering an unfiltered look inside kitchens around the globe. From Michelin-starred restaurants and hidden street food gems showcased in full-length episodes, to POV recipes in short-form episodes, Chef puts viewers in the shoes of the people behind the scenes, offering a unique, captivating perspective for everyone from the culinary obsessed to the simply curious. You can view the first full-length episode, “Inside the World’s #1 Pizza Restaurant” now, only on YouTube, along with the first short-form POV episode, “Butter Chicken Shawarma”. New short-form POV episodes will debut daily across Nick’s newly-debuted @Chef channel with full-length episodes rolling out throughout 2026-27 exclusively on YouTube.

    It has been revealed that morgan Jay | Music Therapy with Morgan Jay | Upcoming series premieres Nov. 18 on Jay’s YouTube channel.

    According to recent reports, music Therapy is an original YouTube series developed and produced by viral comedian and musician Morgan Jay and Ty Stafford of Austin-based creative agency Hello Party, financed by Live Nation Studios. In each episode, Jay plays musical therapist to a celebrity guest, blending unscripted conversation and improv with live songwriting before the pair close with an original song they create together. The result lands somewhere between a talk show, a comedy special and a live concert. The first season features Kam Patterson, Ron Funches, Mara Wilson, Brennan Lee Mulligan, Yung Gravy, Matt Friend, Abbey Romeo, Mark Smalls, Tony Jefferson, ASHBY, Josh Johnson and Mandal Mann. Music Therapy was created by Morgan Jay and Ty Stafford (Hello Party) and is directed by Stafford. Brooke Schley serves as showrunner and co-writes the series with Jay. Executive producers are Graham Sicalowski, Robin Rapino, Stella Bulochnikov, Brooke Schley and Matt Sadeghian.

    In a recent development, emma Chamberlain | What Are You Waiting For? | Latest series premieres early 2027 on Chamberlain’s channel.

    Emma Chamberlain doesn’t like waiting in line – and wants to understand more about people who do. In this upcoming ongoing series, what starts as an investigation of New York City’s most frequented lines unspools into a thoughtful and expansive meditation on subcultures, fandoms, and what makes our modern world tick. At once whimsical, profound and provocative, and underpinned by Emma’s singular POV, What Are You Waiting For? is a hilarious cultural commentary that not only asks what people are waiting for – but why. The series is executive produced by two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner Joe Lewis, with Amplify Pictures (Fleabag, 100 Foot Wave) serving as the co-studio and production tech giant.

    Grace Reiter | Twilight (but better) | New parody film premieres Feb. 18 on Reiter’s channel.

    Comedian, writer, and actor Grace Reiter (Saturday Night Live) is expanding her comedic universe with Twilight (but better), her second unscripted parody film. Reiter first made waves with her viral sketches and The Hunger Games (but better), which debuted on YouTube in November 2025 and has garnered more than 18 million views. Now, alongside her work on SNL and her Netflix series Minimum Wage, Reiter brings her signature blend of spontaneous comedy, sharp satire, and irreverent humor to one of the most iconic franchises of a generation. Twilight (but better) is produced by But Better Productions. Grace Reiter serves as director with Andie Schlenker and Anderson Appleby as producers, and Cindy Schlenker as co-producer.

    Wesley Wang | Three new projects.

    It has been revealed that in this upcoming sci-fi horror short film, a routine welfare check at a remote desert preserve turns terrifying when four park rangers discover an otherworldly presence inside a woman’s tent, leaving the youngest ranger separated from his own body. Response is produced by Wesley Wang Media with Jason Rodelo serving as director and writer.

    It has been revealed that A new six-episode, interactive murder-mystery series that puts viewers in the role of detective, with $100,000 on the line for the first person to crack the case. Told through found footage, digital breadcrumbs and hidden clues woven throughout each episode, the mystery unfolds over six weeks on YouTube, challenging viewers to pause, rewind, decode and collaborate to uncover the truth. The first viewer to correctly solve the case wins $100,000! Extract 14 is directed and written by Wesley Wang and produced by Wesley Wang Media.

    Recent findings suggest that A new series where ten aspiring filmmakers, chosen from thousands of internet strangers, are brought to New York for an immersive, seven-day filmmaking bootcamp where they’ll compete for $100,000 to bring their dream movie to life. Guided by filmmaker Wesley Wang and a panel of Hollywood industry experts, contestants will take on every stage of the filmmaking process, culminating in a red carpet premiere where the viewers get the final say in choosing the grand prize winner. Absolute Cinema is produced by Wesley Wang Media.

    Aryna Sabalenka | Aryna’s Arena: Unfiltered | New series premieres spring 2027 on Sabalenka’s channel.

    According to recent reports, she’s the most dominant tennis player on the planet; and the world can’t look away. Aryna Sabalenka has spent years letting us watch her win. Now cameras follow her everywhere press passes don’t go. A Gucci ambassador designing her own $250K diamond necklace, a bride-to-be planning a wedding while living out of a suitcase for 300+ days a year, a daughter flying home to Belarus between slams, Aryna is building an empire in real time with the whole world watching. From UltraBoom Media, the creators of OFF DAY, a team led by Producers and Creatives from Anthony Bourdain: Parts Unknown, Aryna’s Arena: Unfiltered is an evolution and expansion of Aryna Sabalenka’s YouTube series (Aryna’s Arena). It is a docu-reality series that lives inside her world, on the court, on the road, and everywhere in between, capturing the brand meetings and dress fittings, the late nights with her fiance, and the quiet hotel room moments where she finally gets to just be herself. Raw and glamorous with the playfulness that is uniquely Aryna, this is an unfiltered voyeuristic portrait of power, identity, chaos, and the chosen family around her that makes it all possible.

    Track Star* | Track Star Tonight | Fresh series now live on a dedicated channel; more new episodes to roll out this winter.

    Sources indicate that track Star* is a music-driven digital show hosted by Jack Coyne that brings artists and fans together. Expanding on its popular on-the-street game and Track Star Podcast, Track Star Tonight is a upcoming, intimate live performance series featuring emerging and established artists in front of a small audience, blending live music, storytelling, and artist discovery. Following performances from artists including Remi Wolf, Kings of Leon, The Womack Sisters,  Medium Build, and Florence Road, the series will continue to release new performances and collaborations through the end of 2026 and into 2027. Track Star* is produced by Public Opinion Corporation and created by Jack Coyne, Kieran Coyne and Henry Kornaros.

    Industry observers note that ina Garten | Happy Hour with Ina Garten: Thanksgiving Special | New special premieres Nov. 25 at 6 a.m. ET on Happy Hour with Ina’s channel.

    On November 25, Happy Hour will air a special Thanksgiving episode featuring past guests and friends of Ina, including Bobby Flay, Seth Meyers, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jennifer Garner and, of course, Jeffrey. Ina and her friends will answer listener questions, share Thanksgiving memories, and offer hosting tips to get you inspired before the significant day. Happy Hour is part of the Vox Media Podcast Network. Ina Garten serves as host with Jenna Weiss Berman, Ali Jaffe Ramis and Deborah Davis as executive producers. Kate Tyler is contributing producer, with Jules Natt as producer and Mica Pollan Bahn as associate producer.

    Recent findings suggest that sam Eckholm | Access Granted: Flying with the Royal Air Force Red Arrows | Fresh episode premieres Nov. 27 on Eckholm’s channel.

    According to recent reports, access Granted is a cinematic documentary series that takes cameras to the world’s most secretive places, putting audiences inside demanding missions that have never been seen before. In an upcoming episode, host Sam Eckholm joins the Royal Air Force Red Arrows as Britain’s legendary aerial display team crosses the Atlantic to celebrate America’s 250th birthday, going behind the scenes with the pilots, the engineers, and the crew. Then he straps into the back seat of the lead jet and flies the full display, flying hundreds of miles per hour just a few feet from six other aircraft. Sam Eckholm is the creator and host of Access Granted with JoJo Phillips serving as executive producer and Swayne Martin as producer.

    Jon Youshaei | Created with Jon Youshaei | New episodes premiere this winter on Youshaei’s channel.

    Created with Jon Youshaei is the award-winning docuseries where Jon goes behind the scenes with today’s biggest stars during their biggest moments. Think ESPN’s 30 For 30 docuseries, but about creators and celebrities. All access. No filters. In past episodes, Jon spent 45 days with MrBeast, shadowed Kevin Hart on set, and followed Steph Curry during All-Star Weekend. These upcoming episodes feature Jon as he spends another month on-set with MrBeast for Beast Games season 3 (including filming in the Colosseum in Rome), goes behind-the-scenes with Mark Rober on his newly introduced streaming show, and hits the road with Dude Perfect for their multi-million dollar arena tour. Created is directed and hosted by Jon Youshaei with Amanda Marcovitch serving as producer.

    Recent findings suggest that scott Evans | House Guest Vacay | Newly introduced series premieres Jan. 8 on Evans’ channel.

    Sources indicate that scott Evans is packing his bags and taking House Guest on the road with House Guest Vacay. In this latest series, he’s bringing the laughs, candid conversations and unexpected moments to celebrity getaways across the country and around the world. His first stop in Lagos, Nigeria premieres January 8 exclusively on YouTube. House Guest Vacay is produced by Summer Break Studios and created and hosted by Scott Evans.

    Phil Rosenthal | Somebody Feed Phil | Season 9 premieres spring 2027 on Rosenthal’s channel.

    Opa! Season 9 of Somebody Feed Phil kicks off in a destination long at the top of Phil’s wish list: Greece. On the island of Sifnos, globetrotting foodie Phil Rosenthal finally gets his first taste of the country, with sun-soaked tavernas, fresh-caught seafood and a warm welcome from new friends. It’s the start of a season of great meals, big laughs and more destinations to be revealed. The series won the 2022 Critics Choice Real TV Award for Best Travel/Adventure Show and earned a James Beard Award nomination. Rosenthal is the creator, executive producer and host of Somebody Feed Phil, a two-time New York Times bestselling author, and the creator of the Emmy-winning CBS comedy Everybody Loves Raymond. Somebody Feed Phil is produced by Lucky Bastards in partnership with Banijay Americas and Banijay Rights. Rich Rosenthal serves as executive producer and showrunner.

    Lilly Singh | Eligible Aunties | New series premieres 2027 on Singh’s channel.

    Sources indicate that eligible Aunties is a warm, funny, character-driven unscripted docu-follow series hosted by Lilly Singh that trades shallow villa romances for mature women with real emotional intelligence and emotional baggage. With Singh acting as the ultimate cheerleader and trusted confidante, the show follows a diverse cast of older single women navigating modern dating apps, new romance rules, and their meddling families. Directly serving a rapidly growing demographic of older unmarried adults craving real connections, the series highlights the joy and chaos of putting yourself back on the market. Ultimately, it proves that while finding love doesn’t get easier with age, it definitely gets more interesting. Eligible Aunties is produced by Unicorn Island Productions and created and hosted by Lilly Singh.
